Hunar Adda: Four Crore Résumés and Nobody's Job

Gurugram, Sunday 15 March 2026, 10.50 p.m. The board meets at ten on Monday. Ishita Sengupta has eleven months of funnel data, two versions of the same number, and no idea which of them describes a company.

1. The night before

The Hunar Adda office sat on the fourteenth floor of a glass tower on Golf Course Extension Road, and from Ishita Sengupta's desk on a Sunday night you could see the tail lights on the expressway heading towards Manesar, where a good share of the company's users worked shifts. She had been Senior Vice-President for Product and Growth for nineteen months. She was thirty-eight. She had a board pre-read due at seven the next morning and a slide in it, slide nine, that she had now rewritten eleven times.

Slide nine was supposed to say what Hunar Adda would be held to in FY27. The growth organisation had proposed "5 crore registered jobseekers and 1.4 crore monthly active jobseekers", which was a continuation of the numbers the company had reported to investors since 2023 and which it was on track to deliver. The employer organisation had proposed "₹210 crore of employer revenue at 82 percent gross renewal", which was also a continuation, and which the company was not on track to deliver. Naveen Thomas in Toronto had sent, at 6 p.m. Gurugram time, a one-line message proposing a third: "verified joins per crore of marketing spend". He had attached no slide, because the number, he wrote, was not yet reportable.

Ishita had a printout of Exhibit 1 on the desk and a printout of Exhibit 4 next to it. Exhibit 1 said the funnel was healthy at every stage and improving at three of them. Exhibit 4 said that the eleven employers who together paid Hunar Adda ₹61 crore a year had, between them, confirmed fewer joins in the December quarter than in the same quarter the previous year. Both had been produced by her own organisation, from the same warehouse, in the same week.

At 10.50 p.m. she wrote at the top of a blank page: What is the smallest set of numbers that, if all of them went up, would mean this company is working? Then she sat looking at it, because she could not decide whether the honest answer had five numbers in it, or two, or whether the question was the wrong one because Hunar Adda was not one funnel at all.

2. How Hunar Adda got here

Hunar Adda was founded in Gurugram in 2020 by Kartik Ahuja, a former category head at a large e-commerce company, and Sandeep Kulkarni, an engineer from Pune, on an observation that both had made independently: that India's white-collar hiring market had been solved twice over, by Naukri and by LinkedIn, while the far larger market of delivery riders, warehouse pickers, security guards, sales executives, beauticians, drivers, telecallers and machine operators was still transacted through gate-notices, WhatsApp groups, and consultants who charged the candidate a month's salary.

The product was an Android app in eleven languages. A jobseeker entered a phone number, verified it by OTP, chose a city and a category, and saw jobs. Employers posted roles, bought contact credits, and called candidates. The company took money only from the employer side. By February 2026 it had 4.1 crore registered jobseekers, 1.19 crore monthly actives, about 2.6 lakh employer accounts of which roughly 9,000 were active in any month, and annualised revenue of ₹168 crore.

The decision that constrains everything in this case was taken in September 2022, and at the time it looked like the best decision the company had ever made. Until then, Hunar Adda had required a jobseeker to complete a profile — name, experience, education, language, a short voice introduction — before seeing any job. Ines Brandt, then a contract designer, had argued that the profile wall was costing the company its entire top of funnel, and an experiment proved her right: removing the wall raised the share of installs that reached a job listing from 34 percent to 79 percent, and raised first-day applications by 2.6 times. The wall came down in November 2022. Registration became a phone number and nothing else.

Three consequences followed, of which the company anticipated one. The anticipated one was growth: installs compounded, and Hunar Adda's registered base tripled in fourteen months. The second was that the definition of a user changed without anyone re-deciding it — the metric the company had always called "activation", first application submitted within forty-eight hours of install, now measured a much cheaper act. The third was structural and is the reason Monday's decision is hard: because the profile is optional, Hunar Adda knows the stated occupation of only 38 percent of its registered base, the education level of 31 percent, and the current employment status of almost none of it. The company that knows the most about India's blue-collar labour market cannot describe its own users.

3. The industry around it

By 2026 the Indian blue- and grey-collar hiring market had three sorts of competitor and one non-competitor that mattered more than any of them. Apna and WorkIndia had built large jobseeker bases on a similar model and competed with Hunar Adda for the same employer budgets in the same eight cities. Info Edge's Naukri had moved down-market with a dedicated product and carried a brand no start-up could buy. Staffing companies — TeamLease, Quess and dozens of regional agencies — were not app companies at all but controlled the actual placement of workers at scale, and were simultaneously Hunar Adda's largest customers and its most credible long-term threat. The non-competitor that mattered was the Government of India's National Career Service portal and the Skill India Digital platform, which were free, which no employer relied upon for volume, and which nonetheless set the political expectation that job-matching should not cost a worker anything.

The demand side had concentrated sharply. Quick commerce had become the single largest employer of app-sourced workers in urban India: the dark-store and rider networks operated by Zepto, Swiggy's Instamart, Blinkit and their logistics partners hired continuously, at scale, with attrition rates that made hiring a permanent operating function rather than a project. Reliance Retail and Flipkart's warehousing partners hired in waves before Diwali and again before the Republic Day sales. Zomato's and Swiggy's restaurant partners hired kitchen staff. Hunar Adda's top ten accounts were, with two exceptions, either these companies' staffing vendors or the companies themselves, and they had learned to buy the way procurement organisations buy: on cost per verified outcome, annually, with an audit.

Two regulatory currents bore directly on Monday's decision. The first was the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, whose consent requirements had, since Hunar Adda's compliance rebuild in July 2025, forced the company to obtain a specific, revocable consent before sharing a jobseeker's phone number with an employer. Fifty-six percent of jobseekers granted it at the point of application; the remainder produced an application an employer could see but not call, a category the product team referred to internally as "dark applies" and which Exhibit 1 did not separate out. The second was emigration law: Rakesh Vora's Gulf corridor, described below, required a Recruiting Agent licence from the Protector of Emigrants under the Ministry of External Affairs' eMigrate system for any recruitment of Indian workers for overseas employment. Hunar Adda did not hold one.

Globally, the company's exposure was small and growing fast. Qasr Facilities Group, a Dubai-based facilities-management firm with 14,000 staff across the UAE and Saudi Arabia, had run a pilot with Hunar Adda since August 2025, sourcing housekeeping and technician candidates from Kerala, Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. The pilot had generated ₹4.3 crore of billings in seven months at an average revenue per confirmed join of ₹18,400 — roughly forty times the domestic figure — and had made Rakesh Vora, who sat in New Jersey and covered both the diaspora and the Gulf, the most quoted person in the company's internal forums.

4. The situation in detail

What follows is a timeline of what happened, what the company believed at each point, and what has since turned out to be wrong.

April 2024. Hunar Adda launched Saathi Bulao, a referral programme: a jobseeker who brought three friends who each registered and applied to one job received a ₹100 mobile recharge, paid through a UPI-linked voucher. The belief was that referral would be the cheapest channel in the company's history. The first six months supported it. By March 2025, referral accounted for 38 percent of installs at a blended payout of ₹41 per install against ₹126 for paid media.

August 2024. The growth team began reporting a viral coefficient. The published figure was 0.61. What has since turned out to be wrong is the denominator: the coefficient was computed as referred registrations divided by referring users — that is, by users who had sent at least one invitation — rather than by all users in the cohort. Recomputed on the full cohort in December 2025, the same series gives 0.11. Both numbers have appeared in board material, eight months apart, without either being labelled as a revision.

January 2025. Employer pricing moved from per-post subscriptions to contact credits — an employer bought the right to unlock a candidate's phone number. Revenue rose 44 percent in two quarters. The belief was that the company had found its pricing. What turned out to be wrong is subtler: credits made the employer's cost proportional to applications viewed, so every improvement Hunar Adda made to application volume raised the employer's cost per hire unless match quality rose with it. The company was, without intending to, selling its customers more of the thing they wanted less of.

July 2025. The DPDP consent rebuild shipped. Jobseekers now consented explicitly to their number being shared. Consent rate settled at 56 percent. The product team believed this was a compliance cost with no commercial consequence, because the application metric was unaffected. It is not visible in Exhibit 1 at all, and it is the most likely single explanation for the divergence between Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 4.

October 2025. A staffing vendor for a large quick-commerce network — Hunar Adda's second-largest account, at ₹9.2 crore a year — commissioned its own audit before renewal. It reported that of 41,000 candidate contacts purchased in the September quarter, 63 percent were unreachable on the first two attempts, and that its own cost per join through Hunar Adda had risen from ₹1,480 to ₹2,210 in twelve months. The account renewed, but at a negotiated rate card, and its buyer asked for quarterly join reconciliation as a contract term.

December 2025. Naveen Thomas's team in Toronto ran a holdout on Saathi Bulao in four districts of Uttar Pradesh and two of Telangana, suppressing the bounty for six weeks. Installs in the holdout fell 19 percent; applications fell 11 percent; employer-confirmed joins fell 2 percent, a difference within the noise band of the join-reporting pipeline. The study covered 1.8 percent of the base and was not re-run, because the festive-season freeze began.

February 2026. Shalini Rajaratnam's team completed a telephonic audit of 1,200 jobseekers who had applied in October and November. It found that 22 percent said they had started a job found through the app; 9 percent said they had been called by an employer but had not taken the role; 47 percent said they had not been called at all. The audit was conducted in Hindi and Bhojpuri only, in six northern districts, and the sample was drawn from users who had granted notification consent.

5. The people

Ishita Sengupta, SVP Product & Growth, Gurugram. Position: the company's reported funnel measures the jobseeker's journey up to the point where the employer becomes involved, and then stops. Incentive: she owns both the growth team and the marketplace product team, and her FY27 objectives will be written from slide nine. What she is not saying: she believes the referral programme is close to being a payout for registrations that would have happened anyway, but she approved its budget increase in July and has not found a way to say both things in the same sentence.

Kartik Ahuja, co-founder and CEO, Gurugram. Position: scale is the moat; the company that has every jobseeker in India will eventually be paid by every employer, and 5 crore is a number the market understands. Incentive: he is in early conversations about a Series D at a valuation anchored on user base and growth rate. What he is not saying: an existing investor told him in January that the next round would be priced on revenue quality, and he has not shared that note with the leadership team.

Prerna Salunkhe, VP Growth Marketing, Bengaluru. Position: acquisition is the only part of the business that performs to plan; blended cost per install is ₹94 against a ₹120 plan, and cutting the referral bounty in March, before the pre-monsoon hiring season, would be self-harm. Incentive: her team's quarterly variable pay is calculated on registered users added and blended cost per install. What she is not saying: she has known since November that one OEM pre-install partner's traffic shows a 91 percent day-7 uninstall rate, and she has kept it in the blend because removing it raises her cost per install by ₹11.

Naveen Thomas, Principal Data Scientist, Toronto. Position: only employer-confirmed joins are a real outcome; everything upstream is an intermediate variable, and the company should be managed on joins per crore of spend. Incentive: he has argued this since he joined and his standing rests on the December holdout. What he is not saying: join confirmation depends on employers uploading reconciliation files, which four of the top ten do irregularly and two do not do at all, so his own preferred metric has coverage of about 61 percent of revenue and he cannot presently state the error bar.

Shalini Rajaratnam, Director of Employer Success, Singapore. Position: the company has an unreachability problem, not a volume problem, and every rupee spent on installs before fixing contactability makes the churn worse. Incentive: her team is measured on gross revenue retention, which fell from 88 percent to 79 percent over the year. What she is not saying: two of her largest accounts have asked for a cost-per-join commercial model, and she thinks Hunar Adda would make more money under it — a view that, if stated, would put her in direct conflict with the finance plan she signed in November.

Sandeep Kulkarni, co-founder and VP Engineering, Pune. Position: the instrumentation debt has to be paid before any new metric is adopted; the event that fires on "application submitted" has three code paths, one of which fires on a retry. Incentive: he has eighteen engineers and a mandate to deliver an employer-side applicant tracking module by June that three accounts have been promised. What he is not saying: he estimates the join-reconciliation pipeline Naveen wants would take two engineers for a full quarter, and he has not told Naveen because he does not want the estimate used to make the case for hiring in Toronto rather than Pune.

Ines Brandt, Design Director, Berlin. Position: the profile wall came down for a good reason in 2022 and the answer is not to put it back, but the application flow now optimises for a tap, not for an intention, and the unreachability numbers are the predictable result. Incentive: none financial; she wants the employer-side product, which she regards as unbuilt. What she is not saying: her team's usability study in Kanpur and Nashik found that 31 percent of applicants did not recall applying to the specific role the employer later called them about.

Rakesh Vora, Head of Global Enterprise Sales, New Jersey. Position: the Gulf corridor is worth more per placement than three hundred domestic applications and should get the next two engineering quarters. Incentive: his commission plan pays on new-logo annual contract value, and Qasr Facilities Group has offered a ₹22 crore three-year commitment. What he is not saying: Qasr's commitment is contingent on Hunar Adda holding or partnering for an eMigrate Recruiting Agent licence, and the legal opinion he commissioned in February is more equivocal than his pipeline note implies.

Devraj Bhattacharya, nominee director, Ashvatth Growth Capital, Mumbai. Position: the board wants one headline metric for FY27 and does not much mind which, provided it is not changed again in FY28. Incentive: Ashvatth marked its position up in 2024 on a user-multiple basis. What he is not saying: his fund's own investment committee has begun asking about revenue per active user across the portfolio, and he would welcome a metric change if it arrived as the management team's idea.

7. Voices

"We are the cheapest acquisition engine in Indian internet. Forty-one rupees. If we turn off Saathi Bulao three weeks before the pre-monsoon hiring wave, we will spend the rest of the year explaining a chart that goes down."

8. The options as Ishita sees them

By Sunday evening Ishita had narrowed the slide to three candidate shapes, and had begun to suspect that the narrowing was itself the error.

Option A: hold the line. Commit to 5 crore registered and 1.4 crore monthly active jobseekers for FY27, renew the ₹38 crore media and referral budget, and treat the employer-side softness as a sales execution problem to be fixed with pricing discipline and a rate-card reset. This is the option that requires no re-instrumentation, keeps Prerna's team whole, matches what Kartik has said to prospective investors, and is defensible on Exhibits 1, 2 and 3. Its cost is that it puts another year between the company and any measurement of whether it places people.

Option B: re-base on outcomes. Declare employer-confirmed joins per crore of marketing spend the company's primary metric, cut the referral bounty by half, redirect the saving into field agents and into the join-reconciliation pipeline, and accept that installs and registrations fall in FY27. This is the option Naveen argues for and Shalini would support. Its cost is that the metric it elevates is available for only 61 percent of revenue, depends on data the company does not control, is reported with a lag of up to two months, and would take two engineers a quarter to make trustworthy — during which time the company would be managed on a number it cannot yet see.

Option C: move weight to the Gulf. Take the Qasr commitment, build the overseas corridor, and let the domestic funnel run flat on a maintenance budget. Revenue per placement is forty times domestic and the buyer is sophisticated and contractual. Its cost is the eMigrate licensing position, a concentration risk in a single account, and the fact that the corridor's unit economics rest on seven months of data and 2,300 placements.

What Ishita had written and crossed out twice was a fourth line: that all three options assume the company has one funnel. The numbers the board sees run from install to application and stop. The numbers the customer sees begin at the contact unlock and end at a join. Between them sits the DPDP consent gate, the unreachability rate, the recall problem in Kanpur, and a set of events that Sandeep says cannot presently be joined. It is possible that the honest slide nine has two funnels on it that meet in the middle, with a conversion rate between them that nobody has ever computed — and it is also possible that a board which has asked for one number will not accept a slide with two.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at ten on Monday 16 March 2026 and will approve the FY27 operating plan. The media agency's master agreement lapses on 31 March; the renewal terms on the table require a twelve-month commitment of ₹38 crore with a quarterly reallocation window but no exit. The Saathi Bulao payout can be changed at fourteen days' notice under the voucher partner's contract, but the pre-monsoon hiring wave begins in the last week of April and both quick-commerce staffing vendors have indicated demand roughly 20 percent above last year.

The company held ₹214 crore of cash at the end of February against a monthly net burn of ₹9.4 crore, and Ashvatth's governance rights require board approval for any single marketing commitment above ₹25 crore. Variable compensation for eighty-one people in growth and marketing is written against registered-user and cost-per-install targets for the year ending 31 March; changing the plan mid-year is possible but would require a one-time accrual that finance has estimated at ₹2.1 crore. Sandeep's eighteen engineers are committed to the employer applicant-tracking module promised to three accounts by June; he has said he can release two, not four. Qasr's ₹22 crore offer expires on 30 April and is expressly conditional on a written position regarding recruitment licensing. The DPDP consent architecture cannot be loosened; the only available lever is to make the consent moment more persuasive, which is design work Ines will not be present to do after 10 April.

10. Questions for discussion

1. Take Exhibit 1 at face value. What, precisely, does each stage of that funnel measure about a jobseeker, and at which stage does the measurement stop describing anything an employer would pay for?

2. Exhibits 2 and 3 both flatter the referral channel and Exhibit 4 does not. Reconstruct the argument each exhibit supports, and identify the assumption in each that, if wrong, reverses the conclusion.

3. Exhibit 3 shows referred users retaining best. In a marketplace where a successful outcome removes the user, what should "retention" mean, and what would you instrument to measure it?

4. Hunar Adda has three estimates of placements that differ by a factor of six (Exhibit 5). What would you do in the next four weeks — with two engineers, not four — to make one of them trustworthy, and what would you tell the board in the meantime?

5. Every stakeholder in Section 5 is withholding something. For Prerna, Naveen and Kartik in turn, work out how the metric each proposes would change their own reported performance, and whether a different ownership arrangement for the numbers would change what they say out loud.

6. It is Monday morning. Ishita has forty minutes on the agenda. What does slide nine say, what cadence and owner does she attach to each number on it, what does she ask the board to stop asking her for — and what does she do about the ₹38 crore commitment that must be signed by the thirty-first?

At 12.20 a.m. Ishita closed the laptop and then opened it again. The blank page still had one sentence on it. Below it she had, at some point in the last hour, typed and not deleted a second: the number that would have told us this a year ago was never on the dashboard, and the reason is not that nobody thought of it. She read it twice, decided she could not say that to Devraj Bhattacharya at ten o'clock, and could not think of anything truer to say instead. Outside, the expressway traffic had thinned to the night shift heading for Manesar. Slide nine was still blank.

Nirbhay Insurance Technologies: Where Does the Funnel Leak?

A teaching case. Mumbai, September 2025. ₹12 crore of growth budget, three channels, and five rates that nobody had ever written on the same page.

1. Opening: eleven days

On the evening of 19 September 2025, Aparna Deshpande walked back from the Nirbhay office on Senapati Bapat Marg in Lower Parel, Mumbai, with two documents on her phone. The first was a term sheet from Sampann Pay, a payments application with 4.1 crore monthly users, offering Nirbhay a nine-month exclusive slot in its insurance tab for ₹9 crore. The offer expired on 3 October. The second was a spreadsheet her data scientist in Toronto had sent at 2 a.m. Mumbai time, with a subject line that read: "Before you sign — look at the third row."

Aparna was Head of Product at Nirbhay Insurance Technologies, and she had eleven days. The board met on 30 September to allocate ₹12 crore of the Series B round to growth for the second half of the financial year, and the chief growth officer had already circulated a plan in which ₹9 crore of that went to Sampann Pay before Dhanteras. The company's reasoning was straightforward: Nirbhay needed volume before the festive season, and Sampann Pay could deliver more installs in nine months than Nirbhay's entire field operation had delivered in three years.

What troubled Aparna was not the price. It was that in the eighteen months she had run product, Nirbhay had never once looked at its customer journey as a sequence of rates. It measured installs, it measured gross written premium, and it measured a churn number produced monthly by the finance team. Between the install and the premium lay four other things that could go wrong, and she could not have said, on 19 September, which of the four was costing the company most.

2. Company background

Nirbhay was founded in Nagpur in January 2021 by two former general-insurance executives who had noticed that India's microinsurance problem was not appetite but friction. Their thesis was that a delivery rider in Indore or a tailor in Solapur would buy a ₹59-a-month personal-accident cover if the purchase took ninety seconds, the premium came off a UPI autopay mandate, and the claim could be filed by sending photographs on WhatsApp. By September 2025 the company was licensed by the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India as a corporate agent, underwrote through two partner insurers, and had written ₹128 crore of gross premium in FY25.

The product line had two tiers. The entry product, Nirbhay Suraksha, was a ₹59-a-month accident cover with a ₹5 lakh sum assured, sold almost entirely through the app. The second, Nirbhay Sehat, was a ₹249-a-month hospital top-up that produced roughly four times the contribution of the entry product and was the company's actual business model: acquire cheaply on accident cover, upgrade a minority to health.

It separates rates from magnitudes, because a rate improvement is worth different amounts of money depending on the population it applies to — four points of activation is worth more applied to 7 lakh installs than to 46,000. The defensible claim is not that the path is safe. It is that the funnel tells Aparna which risks she is taking, and the ₹9 crore plan did not.

Pirate Metrics (AARRR)

How does the pirate funnel organise everything I could measure?

A quiet Tuesday, a loud spreadsheet

On the second Tuesday of March 2025, Naveen Kapoor opened the growth dashboard for Manzar Fit, a Pune-based fitness app with guided home workouts and a ₹499-a-month subscription, and found exactly what the board had asked him to explain. App installs for the quarter were up 41 percent over the previous one — 100,000 in the month just closed, against 71,000 the month before — and yet monthly recurring revenue, the number the board actually cared about, had grown by only 6 percent. Someone on the marketing team had already framed this as good news: "installs are the leading indicator, revenue will catch up." Naveen was not sure that was true, and he had eleven days before a board review to find out, with a discretionary Q2 budget of roughly ₹15–20 lakh a month that could go either into buying more installs or into fixing something inside the product.

The trouble was that "growth" as a word covered five or six genuinely different things — how many people found the app, how many of them actually tried it, how many stuck around, how many told a friend, how many paid — and Manzar's dashboard reported all of them as a wall of numbers with no visible relationship to one another. Naveen needed a way to lay the whole customer journey out in one line, see where the number was actually leaking, and argue for a specific rupee decision rather than a vibe. That is precisely the gap the framework he reached for next was built to close.

The idea

The framework is called AARRR — pronounced, deliberately, like a pirate's growl — and it names five stages that any product's users pass through, each with one metric that summarises it: Acquisition (how people find you), Activation (whether they experience real value the first time), Retention (whether they come back), Referral (whether they tell someone else), and Revenue (whether any of this makes money). It was proposed in 2007 by Dave McClure, an investor then running seed accelerator 500 Startups, in a talk titled "Startup Metrics for Pirates," aimed at founders who were reporting a single vanity number — usually installs or registered users — as if it were a business.

McClure's insight was not the five categories themselves, which were already common sense to any retailer; it was the insistence that they be measured separately and in sequence, each as a conversion rate into the next, rather than folded into one blended "growth" figure. The sentence Naveen could say in the boardroom without sounding glib was this: "Installs measure the top of a five-stage funnel; the board's number, revenue, sits at the bottom, and a leak at any stage above it will show up as flat revenue no matter how healthy the top looks." AARRR is a lens for locating that leak, not a metric in itself — nobody's dashboard literally has a field called "AARRR."

How it actually works

Applying the framework starts with a decision practitioners often skip: writing a precise, falsifiable definition for each stage's boundary event, specific to the product, before touching a single number. "Acquisition" for Manzar meant a first app open following an install, attributable to a channel. "Activation" could not simply mean "signed up," because a signup is an administrative act with no evidence of value delivered; it had to mean something the user experienced — Naveen's team settled on completing a full guided workout within 24 hours of install, on the working theory that this was the moment a user learned what the app actually did for them. "Retention" needed a time window and a bar for "active," which the team fixed as logging at least one workout in the fourth week after install — a Day-30-ish check rather than "opened the app," because opening without exercising proves nothing about the product's core value. "Referral" was sharing a personal invite code that led to at least one new install, and "Revenue" was converting to the paid plan, chosen deliberately over "revenue per user" because Manzar needed a conversion count it could multiply against price.

Only once every stage has a definition this concrete does the second step — building the funnel table — mean anything: take one acquisition cohort (all installs in a fixed period), and for each subsequent stage record both the raw count and the rate relative to the stage before it, never relative to the original cohort alone. That distinction matters because a rate against the previous stage tells you where the leak is; a rate against the total only tells you that a leak exists somewhere.

Fig. 1 — Manzar Fit, March 2025 cohort. Each percentage is the conversion rate from the stage immediately above it, not from the original 100,000.

A worked example, then a second pass

Lay Manzar's actual March numbers out stage by stage and the arithmetic is plain. Acquisition: 100,000 installs, at a blended cost of ₹42 lakh in paid media, or roughly ₹42 per install. Activation: 35,000 users completed a workout within 24 hours — a 35 percent activation rate (35,000 ÷ 100,000). Retention: of those 35,000, 8,750 logged a workout in week four — a 25 percent retention rate (8,750 ÷ 35,000). Referral: of the 8,750 retained users, 1,313 shared an invite code that converted at least one friend — 15 percent (1,313 ÷ 8,750, rounded). Revenue: of the same 8,750 retained users, 30 percent, or 2,625 people, converted to the ₹499 plan, producing monthly recurring revenue of 2,625 × ₹499 = ₹13,09,875, call it ₹13.1 lakh.

Now change one input. Suppose the onboarding team removes a forced account-creation screen that currently sits before a user's first workout — a classic activation-stage friction point — and activation rises from 35 percent to 48 percent, while the rates from activation onward (25 percent retention, 30 percent revenue conversion) hold steady, since nothing about the workout itself changed. Activated users rise to 48,000; retained users to 48,000 × 0.25 = 12,000; paying users to 12,000 × 0.30 = 3,600; and MRR to 3,600 × ₹499 = ₹17,96,400 — a gain of roughly ₹4.86 lakh a month, for a one-time design-and-engineering cost Naveen's team estimated at about ₹6 lakh. Reaching that same ₹4.86 lakh MRR gain purely through acquisition, holding all downstream rates fixed, would require roughly 37,000 additional installs a month at the existing ₹42 blended CAC — about ₹15.5 lakh in recurring monthly ad spend. The comparison is the whole argument in one picture.

Fig. 2 — Holding retention and revenue-conversion rates fixed, a 13-point activation gain compounds into 37 percent more retained users and 37 percent more paying users, downstream.

What a newcomer must notice

Activation is a hypothesis, not a fact

Calling something "the activation event" does not make it so. Manzar's team only trusted "workout within 24 hours" after checking, cohort by cohort, that users who hit it were retained at week eight far more often than users who merely signed up. Until you have run that correlation, your activation metric is a guess dressed as a definition.

Retention needs a window, not just a word

"Retention" said without a time frame is meaningless — Day-1, Day-7, Day-30, and "active in week four" are four different numbers that can move in opposite directions in the same month. Pick the window that matches how often your product is meant to be used, and state it every time you quote the figure.

Referral is not the same thing as virality

Referral rate counts how many existing users invited someone; virality, usually expressed as a K-factor, asks whether each invited user goes on to invite enough others to sustain a self-reinforcing loop. A healthy referral rate with a K-factor under 1 is still a paid-acquisition-dependent business, whatever the marketing deck implies.

"Revenue" changes shape with the business model

For Manzar, revenue meant subscription conversions times price. For a marketplace it would be take-rate times transaction volume; for an ad-funded product, impressions times CPM. The stage is universal; the formula behind it is not, and importing someone else's formula without translating it produces nonsense.

The funnel is multiplicative, so where you spend outranks how much

Because each stage's count is the previous stage's count times a fraction, a percentage-point gain low in the funnel (activation) compounds through every stage beneath it, while a gain at the very top (acquisition) only ever adds users at the existing downstream rates. That asymmetry is why Naveen's arithmetic favoured a product fix over more ad spend.

AARRR tells you where the leak is, never why

A funnel table is a diagnostic instrument, not a diagnosis. Knowing that activation is the weak stage says nothing about which screen, copy line, or loading delay is causing users to quit — that requires session recordings, funnel-drop interviews, or a qualitative look most teams are tempted to skip once they have a chart to show.

It assumes a straight line, and real users loop

AARRR treats each month's acquisition cohort as a fresh run through five one-way stages. In practice, a retained or referring user often becomes next month's cheapest acquisition channel — a loop the funnel model does not represent at all, which is exactly the gap the next framework in this sequence, growth loops, is built to close.

Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and scale

AARRR reads most cleanly in a consumer app like Manzar's, where one individual moves through all five stages themselves. In B2B software the stages stretch and split: "acquisition" is a marketing-qualified lead, "activation" may require an administrator and several end users to each reach their own first-value moment before the account counts as activated, and "revenue" is better tracked as expansion or contraction of an existing contract than as a fresh conversion, since the sale often happens once a year, not continuously. In a two-sided marketplace the honest move is to run two separate AARRR funnels, one for buyers and one for sellers, because a healthy buyer funnel sitting on top of a starved seller funnel simply produces buyers who cannot find anything to buy — the framework has to be duplicated, not merely reinterpreted.

Scale changes the mechanics more than the logic. An early-stage team, as Manzar's was in 2025, can track all five stages by hand in a spreadsheet, updated weekly by one analyst. A large company decomposes each stage further — activation split into a dozen granular "aha" candidates tested against retention, revenue split by plan tier and geography — and assigns a named owner to each sub-metric, because at that size no single growth lead can hold the whole funnel in their head the way Naveen still could.

Common mistakes

Chasing installs while activation leaks. Symptom: acquisition numbers climb every board meeting while revenue stays flat, exactly Manzar's starting position. Underlying error: treating the top-of-funnel count as a proxy for business health. Cheapest check: plot each stage's conversion rate over time, not its raw count — a flat or falling rate below a rising top line is the tell.

Calling any early action "activation." Symptom: the activation rate looks impressive, but retention afterwards is poor regardless. Underlying error: picking a convenient, easy-to-log event — usually signup — instead of testing candidate events against later retention. Cheapest check: run the correlation before naming the metric, not after.

Reporting only Day-1 retention. Symptom: cohort curves look healthy in the first week, and the same cohorts have quietly evaporated by week eight. Underlying error: mistaking an early snapshot for the whole retention curve. Cheapest check: always plot retention out to at least eight weeks before declaring the product "sticky."

A referral number nobody owns. Symptom: a referral chart sits on the dashboard, unreviewed, for months. Underlying error: building the funnel table without assigning an owner and a cadence to each stage. Cheapest check: ask what decision was made because of that number last quarter — if the honest answer is "none," the metric is decorative.

What good looks like

By the time Naveen presented, his team had done the unglamorous work the framework demands: they had tested three candidate activation events against week-eight retention and found that "workout within 24 hours" predicted retention roughly twice as well as "account created," so they discarded the weaker definition rather than keep it for convenience. Each stage of the funnel had a named owner — Ritu Desai on the onboarding side for activation, a monetisation lead for revenue — and a standing monthly review where the group looked only at stage-to-stage rates, never totals. When a metric moved, the first question in the room was always which decision it should change, not whether it looked good in a slide.

The decision, and two questions to keep

Naveen recommended redirecting the incremental Q2 acquisition budget — the roughly ₹15.5 lakh a month it would have taken to buy an equivalent revenue gain through installs — into the one-time, roughly ₹6 lakh onboarding redesign that lifted activation from 35 to 48 percent, on the reasoning that a compounding, one-time product fix beats a recurring media cost that a competitor's ad campaign can neutralise the following month. The board approved it. The next thing on Naveen's reading list, and the natural next step from here, is growth loops versus funnels — because AARRR had just shown him where Manzar's leak was, but it had nothing to say about the fact that Manzar's own retained and referring users were quietly becoming next month's cheapest acquisition channel, a compounding effect no funnel diagram, however carefully drawn, can show.

Two questions worth sitting with: if you improved your weakest funnel stage by ten percentage points, would the resulting revenue gain be cheaper to buy through the stage above it, or to earn by fixing the stage itself? And for each metric on your own dashboard — does it have a named owner, and can you name the last decision it actually changed?

Acquisition, activation, retention, referral and revenue, treated as a chain of conditional rates — what the chain genuinely tells you, what it cannot tell you, and where competent practitioners still disagree.

1. Two rooms, one week apart

Monthly recurring revenue from the cohort: ₹9.86 lakh. Against ₹6.25 crore of spend, the payback period was sixty-three months, and the pre-read said so.

Her head of growth read it as proof that acquisition spend must be halved. Her head of engineering read it as proof that the KYC drop-off — 82 percent of installs never reached a first investment — was the only thing that mattered. Both were reading the same five-row table. Nandita had until 27 February to recommend how ₹25 crore of annual growth budget should be split, and she suspected the table was not merely incomplete but actively misleading about the business.

Three weeks later and 900 kilometres south, Sridhar Iyengar, chief product officer of Otla Systems, a Bengaluru company selling warehouse-management software to mid-market third-party logistics firms at an average contract value of ₹15 lakh, faced the opposite complaint. Otla's board had asked for "a pirate funnel, like the consumer companies run." His team built one: 1,850 marketing-qualified leads a quarter, 420 sales-qualified, 96 pilots, 31 closed-won. It was tidy and it explained nothing, because Otla's problem was not new logos. Of ₹46 crore of annual recurring revenue, growth came overwhelmingly from expansion inside the 310 existing accounts, and net revenue retention had drifted from 118 percent to 104 percent over five quarters. No stage in the funnel contained that fact. On 3 March he had to decide whether to keep it, replace it, or do something less comfortable than either.

2. The idea, and the argument it was invented to win

AARRR names five states a user passes through and insists each be measured separately, as a conditional rate into the next: Acquisition (the user arrives), Activation (first real experience of value), Retention (the user keeps coming back), Referral (the user brings someone else), Revenue (money changes hands). It was presented in 2007 by the investor Dave McClure, later a founder of the seed fund 500 Startups, in a talk called "Startup Metrics for Pirates," so named because the acronym reads as a growl.

The categories were not new. The purchase funnel descends from E. St. Elmo Lewis's attention–interest–desire–action sequence of the late 1890s, and direct marketers had segmented on recency, frequency and monetary value since the 1960s. McClure's contribution was polemical rather than taxonomic. In 2007 a founder could say "we have two million users" without being asked which of them had ever received value, returned, or paid. AARRR's real claim is that a blended growth number is an average over five distinguishable populations, uninformative precisely because the five move independently. Eric Ries made the same argument two years later under the heading of vanity versus actionable metrics.

Four schools now disagree about what to do with it, and the disagreements are sharper than the usual framework quibbling.

The operator-pragmatist school holds that AARRR is a filing system and every real problem is a definitional one. It signs: "any scheme that does not separate arrival from first value from return is negligent." It will not sign: "the five stages are ordered, exhaustive, or the right level of aggregation." The retention-first school, associated with mobile-growth practitioners who rearranged the letters into RARRA, holds that acquisition-led sequencing makes teams buy users into a leaking product. It signs: "retention is logically prior; a product without a flattening retention curve should not spend on acquisition at all." It will not sign: "the funnel should be read top-down when planning." The growth-loops school, advanced by Brian Balfour and Casey Winters among others, holds that funnels are the wrong topology: growth is a cycle in which output is reinvested as input, and a funnel cannot represent reinvestment. It signs: "referral and revenue are inputs to acquisition, not terminal stages." It will not sign: "the funnel is a useful planning model for a compounding business." The metric-tree school, visible in the digital-product curricula at Wharton, Haas and Darden, holds that the right structure is a North Star metric decomposed into inputs, sequential or not, every node carrying an owner, a cadence and the decision it informs. It signs: "structure should follow the causal decomposition of the business, not a five-letter mnemonic." It will not sign: "AARRR's stages are independent enough to be owned separately."

3. Mechanics, worked rather than named

Expert practice begins before any number is pulled, with a written definition of each boundary event that is falsifiable, product-specific and versioned. Patang's were: acquisition, first app open attributed to a channel; activation, KYC complete and first investment within seven days; retention, a transaction in weeks five to eight; referral, an invite code redeemed to a completed activation; revenue, conversion to the ₹249 tier. Activation was chosen over "account created" only after the team checked that users who invested within seven days retained at week twelve about 2.4 times as often as users who merely finished KYC. Until that check is run, an activation metric is a guess wearing a definition's clothes.

The formal treatment follows in one line. If N is the acquired cohort, a, r, m the three conditional rates and P the revenue per paying user, then

R = N × a × r × m × P = 2,50,000 × 0.18 × 0.40 × 0.22 × ₹249 = ₹9,86,040

Because the relationship is multiplicative, logarithms turn it into a sum: ln R = ln N + ln a + ln r + ln m + ln P. The consequence is the most misunderstood fact about the pirate funnel. The elasticity of revenue with respect to every stage is exactly one. A one percent relative improvement in installs, activation, retention, paid conversion or price each produce the same ₹9,860 of additional monthly revenue. There is no compounding advantage to being lower in the funnel. The widespread belief that there is comes from confusing percentage points with percentages: moving activation from 18 to 19 is a one-point move but a 5.6 percent relative move, while a point on a 40 percent retention rate is a 2.5 percent relative move. The points are not comparable; the relatives are, and they are equal.

What differs between stages is not leverage but three other things: the price of a relative point, the headroom above the current rate, and whether the improvement is a stock or a flow. Nandita's team priced them.

Two second-order effects are usually left implicit and both bite hard. The first is cross-stage coupling: rates are not independent of volume, because the marginal install is a worse user. When Patang modelled doubling spend, the second ₹6.25 crore bought only 2,10,000 installs (blended cost ₹298) activating at 13.5 percent — 28,350 activated users worth ₹8.79 crore, a ratio of 1.4 against the first tranche's 2.2. Any plan that holds downstream rates fixed while scaling the top is arithmetically wrong. The second is conditioning: every rate after the first is measured on survivors, so tightening activation makes retention appear to rise and loosening it makes retention appear to fall while absolute retained users increase. Both movements are artefacts of the definition, not the product.

4. When the framework holds, stated as tests

AARRR earns its keep when four conditions hold, each testable. One: most users traverse the stages in order. True at Patang — nobody invests before installing. False at Otla, where a procurement-led deal produces revenue before a single end user has activated, and false at Pehredaar Secure, a Noida home-security company whose customers pay ₹5,499 for a camera at a dealer counter weeks before they open the app. Two: the unit of analysis is a single person. True at Patang. False at Otla, where the buying unit is an account of 40 to 300 seats and the activating unit is one warehouse supervisor. Three: rates are stable within a measurement window. True at Patang except when channel mix shifts; false during festival-season media blitzes, when October's funnel and January's describe different populations. Four: revenue per user is roughly constant over the horizon that matters. False at Patang — which is what made the pre-read misleading, because trail income scales with portfolio, so a user worth ₹249 a month in month two is worth about ₹640 by month eighteen. Where condition four fails, the revenue stage must become a cohort revenue curve or the funnel will understate a good business and flatter a bad one.

The framework is actively misleading in three situations: when growth is dominated by a compounding loop rather than purchased flow, because referral is drawn as a terminus rather than an input; when the product is two-sided, because a conversion rate on one side is partly a property of the other side's inventory; and when each stage has a separate owner with a separate bonus, because definitions then become negotiable instruments.

5. Hard edges: seams, sides and machines

Two-sided. Machaan Agri Exchange, a Nashik marketplace renting tractors and harvesters between owners and farmers, found in 2025 that its buyer activation rate was not a buyer property at all. Sorted by machine density within 15 kilometres, first-booking completion ran at 11 percent below eight machines, 27 percent between eight and twenty, and 44 percent above twenty. The buyer funnel was a function of the seller funnel's output. Machaan's error was one blended national funnel; the fix was funnels per district, with local liquidity rather than buyer conversion as the variable under management.

Regulated. Patang's activation stage contains a step Patang does not control: KYC verification runs through an external provider and a central registry, and about 14 percent of failures are third-party timeouts rather than user abandonment. Nandita's team split activation into user-caused and system-caused drop, because a team that cannot separate the two will keep redesigning screens to fix a vendor's latency. Regulated products also restrict experimentation — mandated risk disclosures cannot be tested away — so parts of the funnel are immovable and should be labelled as such.

Hardware plus software. Pehredaar sells 62 percent of units through offline dealers, so the acquisition event is invisible: the company learns a customer exists only if they register the app, which 41 percent do. Revenue, the ₹5,499 hardware sale, precedes activation, and the ₹149 cloud plan converts at 28 percent of registrants. The honest structure is two funnels stitched at an unobservable join, with registration rate treated as a first-class metric because it is the only bridge between channel and product.

AI-native. Praroop AI, a Delhi contract-drafting assistant for mid-sized law firms, defines activation as a first generated draft accepted with fewer than three substantive edits — a probabilistic event, since the same user with the same prompt may activate on Tuesday and not on Wednesday. Two consequences follow. Activation now moves when the model changes, independent of any product decision, so the funnel needs a model-version annotation or its history is uninterpretable. And each draft costs roughly ₹18 of inference, with six percent of users generating 54 percent of that cost, so rising activation and retention can degrade gross margin. The stages are no longer free to improve.

Organisational seams. What mature companies do differs from the diagram they show. Acquisition sits with marketing, activation with growth product, retention with core product, revenue with monetisation — each owner measured on a rate the others move. What works, and Otla, Patang and Machaan converged on versions of it, is a definitional register: every stage event has a written definition, a version number, an owner and a cadence; changes require a stated reason; and every stage owner is also measured on the stage below theirs. It is bureaucratic, and it is the only thing that stops definitional drift.

6. Eight things that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Points are not percentages. The commonest sentence in a growth review — "a point of activation is worth more than a point of acquisition" — is usually false and always ill-formed. In a multiplicative chain every stage has unit elasticity, so a one percent relative gain anywhere is worth the same. An expert hears "a point" and asks "a point of what base?", because a point on an 18 percent rate and a point on a 78 percent rate differ in value by a factor of four. The tell-tale sign is a deck comparing stages with percentage-point deltas on a single axis, which silently privileges whichever stage has the smallest base.

Definition arbitrage is real and quiet. A team under pressure on retention can raise it three points by tightening the activation definition, because retention is conditional on activation and a stricter gate leaves a better-selected survivor pool. The tell-tale sign is several downstream rates improving in the same week with nothing shipped, while the absolute count of retained users is flat or down. The diagnostic is to recompute every rate against the prior quarter's frozen definition. The obvious reading — "our funnel got healthier" — is wrong, because no additional human was served. The same coupling runs the other way: widening the gate lowers measured retention while raising absolute retained users, which is why an expert never reads a rate without the count beside it.

A funnel is a snapshot of a flow, and flows are censored. If activation is measured over seven days, users who installed in the last six days of the month cannot yet have activated, so a naive month-end funnel understates activation by roughly a fifth in a steady month and more in a growing one. The tell-tale sign is an activation rate that dips whenever spend is back-loaded. Experts report cohort-locked funnels — all users acquired in a window, measured only once the window has matured — and accept the reporting lag rather than publish an artefact of the calendar.

Blended rates hide Simpson's paradox. Patang's blended activation fell from 18.9 to 18.0 percent in a quarter during which every individual channel improved, because a cheap high-volume channel activating at 9 percent grew from 8 to 26 percent of installs. The tell-tale sign is a blended rate moving against every disaggregated rate. The obvious reading — "the product got worse" — is backwards: the product got better and the mix got worse, and those call for opposite responses.

Referral is an input, not a terminus. Drawing referral as the fourth stage of a one-way chain conceals that a referred user re-enters at acquisition. Summing the five stage counts therefore double-counts humans, and a referral improvement surfaces in next month's acquisition line, where marketing will claim it. The expert distinction is between referral rate — the share of users who invite — and the K-factor, invites times conversion per invite, which asks whether the loop sustains itself. Patang's 12 percent referral rate sounded healthy; its K-factor of 0.17 meant the business was unambiguously a paid-acquisition business.

Revenue is a curve for accumulating products. Where value compounds with tenure — assets under management, seats, stored data — the revenue stage as a monthly rate is not merely incomplete, it inverts the ranking of businesses. Patang's sixty-three-month payback on first-month MRR became a 2.2-times return on 24-month cohort contribution. The tell-tale sign is a business whose monthly funnel looks unfinanceable while its two-year cohorts look excellent. The obvious reading — "the unit economics are broken" — is wrong; the horizon is.

The order is product-specific. For an e-commerce business revenue occurs at activation: the first purchase is both the value moment and the transaction, and separating them yields two stages with identical numbers and an illusion of diagnostic depth. For a community product referral often precedes retention, because the invited friend is what makes the product worth returning to. An expert redraws the sequence to match the causal order and will defend a four-stage or six-stage chain.

A metric without a decision is decoration. The instrumentation practice taught in the strongest programmes holds that every metric carries an owner, a cadence and the decision it informs. The tell-tale sign of failure is a dashboard tile that has been green for eleven months. The diagnostic takes a minute: name the last budget line, roadmap item or hire that this number changed. If nobody can, it is buying nothing, and the right action is to delete it rather than explain it.

7. How it changes across product types and stages

In consumer products the framework reads most cleanly: one person traverses all five stages and the acquisition event is observable. In B2B and enterprise it splits into two layers that must both be reported — an account-level commercial funnel and a seat-level usage funnel. Otla's data made the case unanswerable.

8. Three worked cases, including one that failed

Patang and the mix. Nandita's team disaggregated the quarter's blended activation decline. One performance network had grown from 20,000 to 65,000 installs a month at 9 percent activation while two others each improved by half a point. Cutting that network's spend by 60 percent raised blended activation from 18.0 to 20.4 percent and cut installs 15.6 percent. Cohort value rose, because the installs removed were worth ₹279 each against a ₹250 acquisition cost — barely above water, and below it after support costs.

Machaan and the district funnel. Machaan stopped buying farmer demand nationally and redirected ₹1.4 crore of a ₹2.2 crore budget into onboarding machine owners in eleven districts in the eight-to-twenty band. Over two quarters those districts reached a mean of 24 listed machines, buyer activation rose from 26 to 41 percent, and completed bookings grew 71 percent on 9 percent fewer farmer acquisitions.

Nukkad Fresh, and how the funnel misled it. Nukkad Fresh, a Bengaluru quick-commerce grocery, ran AARRR with unusual discipline through 2024 and 2025 and nearly died of it. Activation was defined as "first order placed," and the team drove it from 19 to 44 percent — genuinely, measurably — with a ₹150 first-order discount. On the strength of that number the board approved a spend increase, and ₹31 crore went out over two quarters.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Funnels versus loops. The loops position, at its strongest, is not that funnels are inaccurate but that they are the wrong object: a funnel models a one-way flow of purchased attention, while durable companies grow because output is reinvested as input, and a model that cannot represent reinvestment makes teams buy growth they could have compounded. Its evidence is the dominance of loop-driven businesses at scale. It would be wrong if most products' growth were dominated by purchased flow with negligible compounding — empirically true of many perfectly good businesses, including, on the K-factor evidence, Patang.

Retention-first versus acquisition-first. The RARRA position holds that the AARRR ordering makes acquisition the default lever, and that a product without a flattening retention curve should spend nothing on acquisition. Its evidence is the graveyard of well-funded consumer apps with excellent top-of-funnel numbers. It would be wrong wherever retention is structurally low but the economics still work — infrequent, high-value purchases like Machaan's harvest-season rentals, where a three-times-a-year user is a good user and demanding a flat weekly curve would kill a viable business.

Five stages versus a metric tree. The tree position holds that the stages are a mnemonic, not a causal decomposition, and that structure should follow the actual drivers of the North Star metric, which are often non-sequential. Its evidence is the awkwardness of forcing B2B, hardware and marketplace businesses into a consumer sequence. It would be wrong if the mnemonic's communicative value — giving a board, a marketing team and an engineer one shared vocabulary in ten seconds — outweighed its modelling imprecision, which in small organisations it plausibly does.

These are not reconcilable by synthesis. The choice depends on what the measurement is for: to align a twelve-person company, AARRR wins on communication; to allocate ₹25 crore, the tree and the elasticity arithmetic win on precision; to decide what business you are in, the loop question is the only one that matters.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied the framework produces the five-row table and points at the smallest number. Someone who has internalised it does four things differently. They ask what each stage event is defined as, and when the definition last changed, before looking at any value. They convert every proposed improvement into a relative lift and a cost per relative point, so stages become comparable rather than rhetorically ranked. They refuse to read a rate without its count or a blended number without its disaggregation. And they treat the funnel as a diagnostic that locates a leak but never explains one, reaching for session data, support tickets and five conversations with users who dropped — because no arithmetic has ever told anyone why a person closed an app.

12. The decisions

On 27 February, Nandita recommended three things and declined a fourth. She funded the ₹22 lakh KYC-timeout fix, cut the weakest network's spend by 60 percent, and replaced the monthly revenue row in board reporting with a 24-month cohort contribution curve, on the reasoning that a rate cannot describe an accumulating business. She declined a proposal to redefine activation as "KYC complete" — which would have shown 31 percent the following week — because it would improve every number and serve no customer. The board approved the package and rejected the proposed halving of spend, since 2.2-times returns on the inframarginal tranche are not a reason to stop buying.

On 3 March, Sridhar kept a single AARRR funnel for Otla's self-serve tier, where the assumptions hold, and replaced the enterprise funnel with an account-level maturity model centred on seat activation at week six, reported against net revenue retention at month twelve. He removed referral as a stage in favour of customer-sourced pipeline, a number customer success could actually own. He recorded in the planning document that this made Otla's reporting incomparable with the consumer companies the board had in mind, and that the incomparability was the point.

Discussion questions. (1) Patang excludes the 14 percent of KYC failures caused by third-party timeouts. Is a product team right to exclude drop-off it does not control, or does the exclusion guarantee nobody fixes it? (2) Nukkad Fresh's honest redefinition made every reported metric worse. What governance lets a team do that without the CEO losing the next board meeting? (3) When is deleting a stage a sharpening of the model, and when is it the removal of an inconvenient number?
